p.src: Now the Great Sage Sun, leading the horse and carrying the luggage, was roaming the mountaintops calling for his master when Zhu Bajie suddenly came running up in a huff and asked, “Brother, what are you shouting for?” Wukong said, “Master has disappeared. Did you see him?” Bajie said, “I only ever meant to be a monk under the Tang Priest, but you played a trick on me and made me some sort of general. I risked my life fighting that demon for a while and was lucky to escape alive. You and Friar Sand were watching Master, so why ask me?” Wukong said, “Brother, I do not blame you. Somehow your eyes deceived you, and you let the demon return to seize Master. I went to fight the demon and told Friar Sand to guard Master, but now even Friar Sand is gone.” Bajie laughed. “Perhaps Friar Sand has taken Master somewhere to relieve himself.” Before he had finished speaking, Friar Sand appeared. Wukong asked, “Friar Sand, where has Master gone?” Friar Sand said, “Both of you were blind enough to let the demon come back and seize Master. I went to fight that demon, while Master remained sitting on the horse by himself.” Wukong leapt about in fury, crying, “We have fallen for his trick! We have fallen for his trick!” Friar Sand asked, “What trick have we fallen for?” Wukong said, “It was a divide-the-plum-blossom stratagem. He lured us brothers apart and then snatched Master from our very midst. Heavens, heavens, heavens! What are we to do?” Tears streamed uncontrollably down his cheeks. Bajie said, “Do not cry. Crying makes you look like a weakling. In any case, they cannot be far away, only somewhere on this mountain. Let us go and search.”

p.src: When Wukong saw it, he bounded to the entrance in two or three strides. The stone doors were tightly shut, and above them hung a stone tablet bearing eight large characters: “Linked-Ring Cave of Folded Peaks, Hidden-Mist Mountain.” Wukong said, “Bajie, get to work! This is the demon’s lair. Master must be inside.” The fool, emboldened by their strength, raised his rake and struck with all his might, smashing a great hole in the stone door. He shouted, “Monster, send our master out at once! Otherwise my rake will bring down your gate, and your entire household will be finished!”

Wukong said, “Bajie, get to work!
This is the demon’s lair. Master must be inside.”

The fool, emboldened by their strength, raised his rake and struck with all his might, smashing a great hole in the stone door. He shouted, “Monster, send our master out at once! Otherwise my rake will bring down your gate, and your entire household will be finished!”

p.src: The little demon guarding the gate hurried inside to report, “Your Majesty, disaster has struck!” The old demon asked, “What disaster?” The little demon said, “Someone outside has smashed the gate and is clamouring for his master!” The old demon exclaimed in alarm, “I wonder who has tracked us here?” The vanguard said, “Do not be afraid. Let me go out and see.” The little demon hurried to the front gate, cocked his head, and peered through the hole. Seeing a creature with a long snout and great ears, he turned and called loudly, “Your Majesty, do not fear him! It is only Zhu Bajie. He has little ability and will not dare behave outrageously. If he does, we shall open the gate, seize him, and steam him with the others. The only one to fear is that monk with the hairy face and thunder-god’s beak.” Hearing this from outside, Bajie said, “Brother, he is not afraid of me—only of you. Master must be in there. Hurry forward.” Wukong cursed, “You vile beast! Your Grandpa Sun is here. Send my master out, and I may spare your life!” The vanguard said, “Your Majesty, this is terrible! Sun Wukong has tracked us here too.” The old demon complained, “This is all because of that ‘divide-the-petals’ scheme of yours. Now you have brought disaster to our very gate. How are we to settle this?” The vanguard said, “Set your mind at ease, Your Majesty, and do not complain yet. As I recall, Sun Wukong is a broad-minded and magnanimous monkey. Though his magic powers are immense, he dearly loves flattery. Let us take out a false human head to deceive him, flatter him a little, and say that we have eaten his master. If we can fool him into leaving, the Tang Priest will remain ours to enjoy; if we cannot, we shall deal with him then.” The old demon asked, “Where are we to find a false human head?” The vanguard said, “Just let me make one and see.”

p.src: That fine demon took a solid steel axe and hacked a willow root into the likeness of a human head. He splashed it with human blood until it was a grisly mess, then had a little demon carry it on a lacquer tray to the gate and call, “Grandpa Great Sage, calm your anger and allow me to report.” Sun Wukong truly was fond of flattery. Hearing himself addressed as “Grandpa Great Sage,” he immediately stopped Bajie and said, “Do not strike yet. Let us hear what he has to say.” The little demon holding the tray said, “Your master was seized by our king and brought into the cave. The little demons within are crude and unruly and know no restraint: one came to swallow him, another to gnaw him; some clawed and others bit, until they ate your master entirely. Only his head remains here.” Wukong said, “If he has been eaten, so be it. Just bring out the head and let me see whether it is genuine.” The little demon tossed the head out through the hole in the gate. At the sight of it, Zhu Bajie began to weep. “How pitiful! Such a master went in, and such a master has come out!” Wukong said, “Fool, first examine whether it is real or false, and then you may cry.” Bajie said, “Do not be absurd. How can a human head be real or false?” Wukong said, “This is a false head.” Bajie asked, “How can you tell it is false?” Wukong said, “When a real human head is thrown out, it lands with a dull thud and makes no ringing sound; a false head sounds like a wooden clapper when it lands. If you do not believe me, let me throw it so you can hear.” He picked it up and dashed it against a rock, where it rang out with a loud clang. Friar Sand said, “Brother, it rang.” Wukong said, “Since it rang, it must be false. I shall make it reveal its true form for you to see.” He swiftly drew his gold-banded staff and smashed the thing apart with a single blow. When Bajie looked, he saw that it was nothing but a willow root. Unable to contain himself, the fool began cursing. “You pack of hairy brutes! You have hidden my master inside the cave and tried to fool your Ancestor Zhu with a willow root. Do you imagine my master was transformed from a willow spirit?”

p.src: The little demon who had carried the tray was so frightened that he ran trembling back to report, “Hard, hard, hard! This is hard indeed!” The old demon asked, “Why so many ‘hards’?” The little demon said, “Zhu Bajie and Friar Sand were fooled, but Sun Wukong is an antiques dealer—he knows his goods, he knows his goods! He recognized at once that it was a false human head. If we give him a real head now, perhaps he will leave.” The old demon asked, “How are we to obtain a real human head? There are more heads than we can eat in our Skinning Pavilion. Choose one from there.” The demons went at once to the pavilion and selected a fresh head. They had all the scalp gnawed clean until it was slick and bare, then sent it out on the tray once more, calling, “Grandpa Great Sage, the head before was indeed a false one. This truly is Lord Tang’s head. Our king had kept it as a talisman for the dwelling, but now presents it especially to you.” With a thump, they tossed the human head out through the hole in the gate once more, and it rolled about dripping blood.

p.src: Sun Wukong recognized it as a real human head and, helpless with grief, began to weep; Bajie and Sha Wujing also burst into loud lamentation. Bajie said through his tears, “Brother, do not weep just yet. The weather is none too fine, and I fear the head may soon begin to stink. Let me take it away and bury it while it is still fresh; then we can mourn.” Wukong said, “That makes sense.” The fool, heedless of the filth, clasped the head to his breast and ran to a sunny place atop the cliff. Finding a sheltered spot where the vital airs gathered, he dug a pit with his rake, buried the head, and raised a grave mound over it. Only then did he call to Wujing, “You stay here and mourn with Brother while I find something to make an offering.” He went down by the stream, broke off several large willow branches, and picked up a few pebbles. Returning to the grave, he planted the willow branches on either side and piled the pebbles before it. Wukong asked, “What is the meaning of this?” Bajie replied, “These willow branches will serve as pines and cypresses to shade Master’s grave; and these stones will serve as cakes for an offering to him.” Wukong shouted, “You oaf! The man is dead, yet you offer him stones!” Bajie said, “It shows the feelings of the living and stands for a filial heart.” Wukong said, “Enough of this foolishness. We shall leave Wujing here, both to keep vigil at the grave and to guard the luggage and horse. You and I will smash open their cave, seize the demons, tear them limb from limb, and avenge Master.” Sha Wujing said with tears falling, “Eldest Brother speaks most rightly. You two take care; I shall stand guard here.”

p.src: Good Bajie at once stripped off his black brocade robe, tightened his close-fitting underclothes, raised his rake, and followed Wukong. Putting forth all their strength, the two charged straight ahead without parley, smashed down the stone gate, and cried with a roar that shook the heavens, “Give us back the living Tang Monk!” Every demon in the cave, great and small, was frightened out of his wits, and all blamed the vanguard for bringing this upon them. The old demon asked the vanguard, “These monks have broken through our gate. How are we to deal with them?” The vanguard replied, “The ancients put it well: ‘Once your hand is in the fish basket, you cannot escape the stink.’ What is begun must be finished. Let the commanders on both flanks lead our troops out to kill those monks.” Hearing this, the old demon saw no other course and duly gave the order: “All of you, unite your hearts, take up your finest weapons, and follow me into battle.” With a united battle cry, they charged out through the cave entrance.

p.src: The Great Sage and Bajie hastily fell back several paces to level ground on the mountainside. There they checked the demon horde, and Wukong shouted, “Which of you is the leader whose name is known? Which is the demon who seized our master?” The demons formed their encampment and flourished a splendid embroidered banner. The old monster, iron cudgel in hand, answered in a loud voice, “You insolent monk, do you not recognize me? I am the Great King of South Mountain and have roamed freely here for several hundred years. Your Tang Monk has already been caught and eaten by me. What can you do about it?” Wukong cursed him: “You brazen ball of fur! How old can you possibly be, that you dare lay claim to the name ‘South Mountain’? Lord Laozi, ancestor of the creation of heaven and earth, still sits to the right in the Realm of Supreme Purity; the Buddha Tathagata, the World-Honored One who governs the age, still sits beneath the Great Peng; and Sage Confucius, supreme teacher of the Confucian way, is called merely ‘the Master.’ Yet you vile beast dare call yourself the ‘Great King of South Mountain’ and boast of roaming free for centuries! Do not run! Take a stroke of your venerable grandfather’s staff!” The demon twisted aside to evade the blow, braced his cudgel against the iron staff, and asked with eyes bulging, “Your face has the look of a monkey, yet you dare overwhelm me with so many words? What abilities have you, that you should run riot before my gate?” Wukong laughed and said, “You nameless brute! So you truly do not know old Sun. Stand fast, summon your courage, and listen while I tell you:

p.src: When the Great Sage Sun saw how fiercely the lesser demons fought and that repeated blows could not drive them back, he used his art of multiplying bodies. Plucking out a handful of hairs, he chewed them in his mouth, spat them out, and cried, “Transform!” They all changed into his own likeness, each wielding a gold-banded staff, and drove inward from the front. The hundred or two hundred lesser demons could not guard the rear while attending to the front, nor shield the right while covering the left. Each fled for his life, retreating in defeat to the cave. Wukong and Bajie fought their way outward through the ranks. The luckless demons who failed to see which way the wind blew were met by the rake and bled from all nine orifices; those struck by the staff had flesh and bones mashed to pulp. Terrified, the Great King of South Mountain rolled up wind and raised a mist, escaping with his life. The vanguard had no power of transformation and was soon felled by a stroke of Wukong’s staff. Revealing his true form, he proved to be an iron-backed gray wolf demon. Bajie stepped forward, seized him by the legs, turned him over for a look, and said, “From the time he was little, this wretch must have stolen and eaten no end of other people’s piglets and lambs.” Wukong shook himself and recalled his hairs, saying, “You fool, we must not delay. Hurry after the old monster and make him pay for Master’s life.” Bajie looked back and, seeing none of the little Wukongs, said, “Brother, all those manifestations of yours are gone.” Wukong said, “I have already taken them back.” Bajie exclaimed, “Marvelous! Marvelous!” Delighted, the two returned victorious.

p.src: Now the old monster, having escaped alive to his cave, ordered the lesser demons to carry stones and earth and seal the front entrance. The lesser demons who had survived trembled one and all. They blocked the gate completely and dared not show their heads again. Wukong led Bajie in pursuit to the entrance and shouted a challenge, but no one inside answered. When Bajie struck with his rake, he could not budge it in the least. Wukong understood and said, “Bajie, do not waste your strength. They have blocked the entrance.” Bajie said, “If the entrance is blocked, how can we avenge Master?” Wukong replied, “Let us return to the grave for now and see how Wujing is faring.”

p.src: The two returned to the same place and found Sha Wujing still weeping. Bajie grew more sorrowful still. Dropping his rake, he threw himself upon the grave, beat the earth with his hands, and wailed, “O my ill-fated Master! O Master who died far from home! Where shall we ever see you again?” Wukong said, “Brothers, do not grieve so bitterly just yet. The demons have blocked the front entrance, so there must surely be a rear entrance by which they come and go. You two remain here while I go and search again.” Bajie said through his tears, “Brother, be careful! Do not let them take you too, or we shall not know how to do our weeping: one cry for Master and one for Elder Brother, until our lamentations are all in confusion.” Wukong said, “Never fear. I have ways of my own.”

Bajie said through his tears, “Brother, be careful! Do not let them take you too, or we shall not know how to do our weeping: one cry for Master and one for Elder Brother, until our lamentations are all in confusion.”
Wukong said, “Never fear. I have ways of my own.”

p.src: The Great Sage put away his cudgel, tightened his robe, and strode off. As he rounded the hillside, he suddenly heard the murmur of water. He turned to look and saw that it was water in the ravine, rushing down from upstream. Across the ravine he also saw a small gate, with a hidden drain discharging water to its left. “No question about it!” he said. That must be the back gate. If I go there in my true form, some little fiend may open the gate, see me, and recognize me. I had better turn into a water snake and slip across. Wait—if I become a water snake, my master’s departed spirit may learn of it and reproach me, a monk, for taking the long, coiling shape of a snake. I shall become a tiny crab instead. No, that will not do either. Master may blame a monk like me for having too many legs.” He therefore changed into a water rat, darted across with a swish, and crawled through the drain into the courtyard within. Poking out his head to look, he saw a little fiend in a sunny spot, laying out chunks of human flesh one by one to dry. Pilgrim thought, “You wretch! That must be flesh left over from eating Master, dried to keep for rainy days. If I reveal my true form, rush forward, and kill him with one blow, I will merely show courage without strategy. I had better change again, go farther inside, and find the old monster to see how matters stand.” He leapt out of the drain, shook himself, and changed into a winged ant. Indeed:

p.src: He spread his wings and, leaving neither sound nor trace, flew straight into the central hall. There he saw the old monster sitting in vexation and distress, when a little fiend bounded in from the rear and reported, “Great King, wonderful news!” “Where has this good news come from?” asked the old monster. The little fiend replied, “Just now, while keeping watch by the ravine outside the back gate, I suddenly heard someone weeping loudly. I climbed to the peak and looked, and there were Zhu Bajie, Sun Wukong, and Friar Sand, bowing before a grave and wailing bitterly. They must have mistaken that man’s head for Tang Sanzang’s, buried it, and heaped up a grave to mourn over.” Listening unseen, Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “From what he says, my master must still be hidden somewhere and has not yet been eaten. I shall search again and find out whether he is alive or dead before dealing with this monster.”

p.src: The Great Sage flew about the central hall, looking east and west, until he noticed a small side door that was tightly shut. He squeezed through a crack in the door and found beyond it a large garden, from whose depths came the faint sound of lamentation. He flew straight into its depths and saw a grove of great trees. Two men were tied beneath them, and one was none other than Tang Sanzang. At the sight, Pilgrim could no longer contain himself. He resumed his true form, went close, and called, “Master!” Recognizing him, the elder shed tears and said, “Wukong, have you come? Quickly, save me! Wukong! Wukong!” Pilgrim said, “Master, do not keep calling my name. There are others nearby, and word may get out. Since you are still alive, I can save you. That monster claimed he had eaten you and fooled us with a false head, so we have been locked in a bitter struggle with him. Set your mind at ease, Master, and endure a little longer. Once I have brought that fiend down, I can come and free you properly.”

p.src: The Great Sage recited a spell, shook himself, and became an ant once more. Returning to the central hall, he clung to the main roof beam. He saw the little fiends who had survived milling together in clamorous crowds. Suddenly one of them leapt from the throng and reported, “Great King, when they found the gate blocked and could not break it open, they gave up all hope, abandoned Tang Sanzang, and made a grave for the false head. They will mourn all day today, mourn again tomorrow, and on the day after that complete the third day of rites; then they will surely go away. Once we learn that they have dispersed, we can bring Tang Sanzang out, slice and chop him fine, fry him with plenty of spices, and all enjoy a fragrant piece. Then we too shall gain long life.” Another little fiend clapped his hands and said, “No, no! He will taste better steamed.” Another said, “Boiling him will save firewood too.” Yet another said, “He is a rare delicacy. We should salt and cure some of him so that he will last longer.” Hearing this from the beam, Pilgrim flew into a rage. “What deep grievance has my master ever borne you, that you scheme so relentlessly to eat him?” He plucked out a handful of hairs, chewed them to pieces, and blew them gently away. Secretly reciting a spell, he made them all become sleep insects and cast them onto the fiends’ faces. Each insect crawled into a nostril. The little fiends gradually began to nod, and before long they had all fallen asleep. Only the old monster could not sleep soundly. He rubbed his head and scrubbed his face with both hands, sneezing without cease and pinching his nose. “Can he have noticed something?” thought Pilgrim. I shall give him a double dose.” He plucked another hair, worked the same transformation, and tossed it onto the monster’s face, where it entered his nostril. Of the two insects, one went in through the left nostril and the other through the right. The old monster rose, stretched his back, yawned twice, and then fell asleep with a rumbling snore.

p.src: Pilgrim rejoiced in secret. Only then did he leap down and resume his true form. He took the cudgel from his ear and gave it a shake, making it as thick as a duck’s egg. With a resounding clang he smashed through the side door, ran into the rear garden, and shouted, “Master!” “Disciple, come quickly and untie these ropes,” said the elder. “They are cutting me to pieces.” Pilgrim said, “Do not be impatient, Master. Let me kill the fiends first, and then I shall come back to untie you.” He hurried back to the central hall and raised his cudgel to strike, but then checked his hand. “No, I had better free Master first and come back to beat them.” He returned to the garden, only to reconsider: “I had better beat them first and then come back to save him.” After going back and forth like this two or three times, he finally came skipping and capering into the garden. Seeing him, the elder found joy amid his sorrow and said, “Monkey, I suppose you are so delighted to see that I have not been killed that you cannot contain yourself, and that is why you dance about so?” Pilgrim came forward at last, untied the ropes, took his master by the arm, and started away. Then the man tied to the tree opposite called out, “My lords, in your great mercy, please save my life too!” The elder stopped and called, “Wukong, untie that man as well.” “Who is he?” asked Pilgrim. The elder replied, “He was captured and brought here a day before me. He is a woodcutter. He says that he has an aged mother who must be longing desperately for him. He is a truly filial son, so you may as well save him too.”

p.src: Pilgrim did as he was told and untied the woodcutter too. He led them both out through the back gate, up the rocky cliff, and across the steep ravine. The elder thanked him. “Worthy disciple, it is thanks to you that both he and I are alive. Where are Wuneng and Wujing?” “They are both over there mourning for you,” Pilgrim replied. Call out to them.” The elder raised his voice and called loudly, “Bajie! Bajie!” The idiot, dazed from weeping, wiped his nose and tears and said, “Friar Sand, Master’s spirit has come home to appear to us! Is that not him calling us over there?” Pilgrim stepped forward and shouted, “You blockhead! What spirit are you talking about? Is that not Master himself coming toward you?” Friar Sand looked up and saw him. He hurriedly knelt before the elder and said, “Master, how terribly you must have suffered! Elder Brother, how did you manage to rescue him?” Pilgrim then told them the whole story of what had happened.

p.src: When Bajie heard this, he ground his teeth in fury. Unable to restrain himself, he raised his rake, smashed the grave mound flat, dug out the man’s head, and pounded it to a pulp. The Tang Monk said, “Why did you smash him?” Bajie replied, “Master, I do not even know whose dead kinsman he was, yet they made me weep over him.” The elder said, “You have him to thank for saving my life. When you brothers attacked their lair and clamored for them to hand me over, they must have brought him out to pass off as me; otherwise, they would have killed me instead. Bury him again, so that we may show the compassion proper to men of religion.” Hearing the elder’s words, the fool buried the bundle of mangled flesh and bones and heaped up another grave mound.

p.src: Wukong laughed and said, “Master, please sit here a while and wait for me to wipe them out.” He leaped down the rocky cliff again, crossed the stream, and entered the cave. Taking into the central hall the ropes that had bound the Tang Monk and the woodcutter, he found the old demon still asleep, tied all four of his limbs together, scooped him up with the golden-hooped staff, hoisted him onto his shoulder, and went straight out through the rear gate. Seeing him from afar, Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, you do love carrying things in your arms. Would it not be better to find another fellow and carry him between you on a pole?” Wukong came up and set the demon down, whereupon Bajie raised his rake to strike. Wukong said, “Hold! There are still lesser demons in the cave who have not been caught.” Bajie said, “Brother, take me inside and let me fight them.” Wukong said, “Fighting them would take more trouble. Better to find some firewood and root them out for good.” Hearing this, the woodcutter led Bajie to a hollow in the east, where they gathered broken bamboo tips, withered pine foliage, hollow willows, uprooted vines, yellow mugwort, old reeds, rushes, and dry mulberry wood. They collected several loads and carried them in through the rear gate. Wukong set it alight, while Bajie flapped his ears to fan the flames. The Great Sage leaped up, shook himself, and recovered the hairs that had become sleep-inducing insects. By the time the lesser demons awoke, smoke and flames were raging everywhere. Pitiful indeed! Not one of them could hope to escape alive. Even the entire cave dwelling was burned clean away. They then returned to see their master. When the master heard the old demon awaken and cry out, he called, “Disciples, the fiend is awake!” Bajie stepped forward and killed the old monster with one blow of his rake. It revealed its true form: a leopard spirit with a mottled, mugwort-leaf-patterned hide. Wukong said, “A spotted leopard can devour tigers, and now this one could even transform into a man. Only by beating it to death have we ended the threat for good.” The elder thanked them without end and mounted his horse. The woodcutter said, “My lords, my humble home lies not far to the southwest. Please come there and meet my mother, so that we may bow in thanks for saving my life and then see you on your way.”

p.src: In the distance they saw an old woman leaning against a brushwood gate, her eyes brimming with tears as she wailed bitterly, crying for her son and calling upon Heaven and Earth. When the woodcutter saw his mother, he left the elder behind, hurried ahead to the brushwood gate, knelt, and cried, “Mother, your son has returned!” The old woman seized him in an embrace and said, “My son! When you did not come home these past few days, I thought the lord of the mountain had taken you and killed you. The anguish was more than I could bear. Since you were not harmed, why have you only returned today? And where are your carrying rope, pole, and axe?” The woodcutter kowtowed and said, “Mother, I truly was seized by the lord of the mountain and tied to a tree, and scarcely escaped with my life. Fortunately, these honored lords came to my aid. This venerable lord is an arhat from the Tang realm in the Eastern Land, journeying to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. He too was seized by the lord of the mountain and tied to a tree. But his three mighty disciples, whose magic powers are vast, beat the lord of the mountain to death. It proved to be a leopard spirit with a mottled, mugwort-leaf-patterned hide. They burned every one of the lesser demons to death, then untied and rescued that venerable elder, and freed your son as well. Their kindness is truly as boundless as Heaven is high and Earth is deep. Without them, your son would undoubtedly be dead. Now peace has returned to the mountain; even if I travel all night, no harm will come to me.”

p.src: Hearing this, the old woman bowed at every step as she went to welcome the elder and his four-member company, then ushered them all through the brushwood gate and seated them in the thatched cottage. Mother and son kowtowed and thanked them over and over, then hurriedly prepared a vegetarian meal to express their gratitude. Bajie said, “Brother Woodcutter, I know your household is poor. A simple meal will suffice; you must not put yourself to the trouble of making elaborate preparations.” The woodcutter said, “To tell you the truth, my lord, we are indeed poor here in the mountains. We have no fragrant mushrooms, common mushrooms, Sichuan pepper, or other fine seasonings—only a few kinds of wild greens to offer you as a small token of our gratitude.” Bajie laughed and said, “Forgive us for troubling you, forgive us. Just bring it quickly—we are hungry.” The woodcutter said, “It is coming at once, at once.” Sure enough, before long the tables and stools were wiped and set out, and several dishes of wild greens were brought in. This was what they saw:

p.src: Hearing this, the woodcutter said, “My lord, please do not be anxious. Follow this main road westward for less than a thousand li, and you will reach the kingdom of India, the land of utmost bliss.” Hearing this, the elder swung down from his horse and said, “Thank you for coming so far with us. Since this is the main road, please return home, Brother Woodcutter, and convey my deepest respects to your venerable mother. We imposed greatly upon you for that fine vegetarian meal, yet this poor monk has nothing with which to repay you. I can only recite scriptures morning and evening and pray that mother and son may live in peace and enjoy a hundred years of longevity.” The woodcutter repeatedly assented, bade them farewell, and returned by the way he had come. Master and disciples then continued straight westward. And so it was that:
